newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambia says confident donors will lift aid squeeze.
newsitem.headline: Zambia says confident donors will lift aid squeeze.

text.p: Zambian Finance Minister Ronald Penza said on Wednesday he was confident Western creditors would lift an aid squeeze on his government at a meeting on July 9.
Penza said the Zambian government had complied with most reform measures demanded during an earlier meeting of the Consultative Group.
"We are determined to restore normal and positive relations with the donors. We are doing everything we agreed to with our cooperating partners," Penza told Reuters in an interview.
"Assuming that everything remains in order, we are confident of a positive outcome of the Consultative Group meeting," he added.

Western governments tightened aid flows to the southern African country in protest against constitutional changes enforced by the Frederick Chiluba government ahead of a general election last November.
Seven political parties boycotted the polls, which Chiluba's ruling Movement for Multiparty Democracy (MMD) won.
Chiluba is anxious to restore normal relations with donors. He is banking on them to fund a third of the country's $1.1 billion budget for 1997.
Penza said Zambia needed about $200 million in balance of payments support and $275 million in project financing in 1997.
The government resumed dialogue with donors in April and agreed to drop plans to control local and foreign media and to resume talks with opposition parties.
Donor demands for reform of the civil service and maintainance of a budget surplus are targets, Penza said. The country recorded a budget deficit in the first quarter of 1997.
Penza said the government had met most of the conditions demanded by donors in April.
"We are working with the World Bank to draw up a document on civil service reform that will be acceptable to most donors," he said.
"We will certainly see a budget surplus in the second quarter, as well as an overall surplus," he added.
Government dialogue resumed this week with representatives of the 12 opposition parties to lay the ground for a conference of party leaders.
International Monetary Fund (IMF) representative Alwaleed Taha said the Consultative Group meeting was likely to focus on the country's economic performance over the past few months.

"The outcome of the Consultative Group meeting will depend on many factors, including presentation by the government on progress in the economic growth, monetary and budgetary developments, inflation, exchange rates, and donor assesments,' Taha said.
The economy has been stable for the past several months, with the local currency firm at around 1,300 to the dollar, and annual inflation dropping to 24 percent in May from 35 percent in January.
